# VMware/Broadcom Post-Acquisition Pricing Benchmarks

· Last updated May 2, 2026

FFBy [Fredrik Filipsson](/pages/author-fredrik-filipsson), Cofounder · 21 years of software negotiation experience. [Connect on LinkedIn →](https://www.linkedin.com/in/fredrikfilipsson/)

Published: April 3, 2026 Reading time: 11 min Cluster: Vendor-Specific Pricing Category: Infrastructure Software

Broadcom's acquisition of VMware in late 2023 triggered one of the most disruptive enterprise software pricing changes in recent memory. Broadcom eliminated VMware's perpetual licensing model, discontinued hundreds of standalone products, and restructured the portfolio into bundled subscription offerings, VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) and VMware vSphere Foundation (VVF). For most enterprises, this transition resulted in significant cost increases. This benchmark analysis covers what enterprises are actually paying in 2026, what's negotiable, and what alternatives are realistic. For broader vendor benchmarking strategy, see our [Vendor-Specific Pricing Benchmark Deep Dives](/blog/vendor-specific-pricing-benchmark-deep-dives) guide.

**Important context:** VMware post-Broadcom pricing has been extraordinarily volatile. The benchmarks in this article reflect data from enterprise negotiations completed in 2025 to 2026. Organizations renewing before this period may have significantly different baseline pricing.

## The New VMware Product Structure Under Broadcom

Broadcom reorganized VMware's portfolio into two primary offerings that most enterprise customers are being migrated to:

**VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF)** is the full-stack SDDC offering that bundles vSphere, vSAN, NSX, and Aria (formerly vRealize) management suite. VCF is positioned as the flagship enterprise offering and is heavily pushed for organizations with more than 100 cores. VCF includes all the major VMware workloads most enterprises rely on for virtualization infrastructure.

**VMware vSphere Foundation (VVF)** is a stripped-down offering that includes vSphere (compute virtualization) and vCenter (management) without vSAN or NSX. VVF is primarily for organizations that use external storage (SAN, NAS) and do not need software-defined networking. VVF is priced lower than VCF but represents a meaningful reduction in capability versus prior VMware deployments that included vSAN or NSX components.

**What was eliminated:** Broadcom discontinued most standalone VMware products including standalone vSAN, standalone NSX, Horizon View (desktop virtualization) as a separate SKU, and many of the Aria/vRealize modules sold individually. Organizations that purchased these products separately now face re-purchasing them bundled in VCF at higher total cost, or migrating to alternatives.

## VMware/Broadcom Pricing Benchmarks: What Enterprises Pay

[VMware](/vendors/vmware) post-Broadcom pricing is quoted per core per year on a subscription basis. List pricing (as of early 2026) for VCF is approximately $175 to $240/core/year depending on support tier. For VVF, list pricing is approximately $70 to $95/core/year. These list rates serve as the baseline for negotiation; actual enterprise prices are substantially lower after commitment discounts.

| Product | List Price (Per Core/Year) | Enterprise Negotiated Range | Large Enterprise (>10K cores) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) | $175 to $240 | $110 to $165/core/year | $85 to $120/core/year |
| VMware vSphere Foundation (VVF) | $70 to $95 | $45 to $68/core/year | $35 to $52/core/year |
| VMware Tanzu (Kubernetes) | $50 to $120 | $30 to $85/core/year | $25 to $65/core/year |
| VMware Horizon (VDI) | $25 to $45/user/year | $18 to $35/user/year | $12 to $25/user/year |

The discount ranges above reflect negotiated enterprise agreements. Broadcom has significantly less flexibility than legacy VMware on pricing

# Broadcom Q4 2025 Earnings: 8 Things To Know From AI Strength, VMware Growth To Anthropic Deal Reveal

A focus on the accelerators, networking, and other components needed to build infrastructures, plus the signing of huge deals like the new $11 billion sale to Anthropic on top of a massive and growing backlog spike optimism on the future of Broadcom, President and CEO Hock Tan told analysts after his company’s fiscal year 2025 financial report.

Broadcom, the Palo Alto, Calif.-based designer and producer of chips and infrastructure software, reported fiscal year 2025 total revenue growth of 24 percent over that of fiscal 2024, led by a huge growth in its AI semiconductor and its VMware businesses.

Broadcom President and CEO Hock Tan, in both his prepared remarks for the company’s fiscal year 2025 financial report and his responses to financial analysts’ questions on Thursday, painted a picture of a company for whom AI shows no limits to growth.

Tan said Broadcom’s fiscal fourth quarter AI semiconductor business grew 74 percent year-over-year, with custom AI semiconductor sales doubling over last year.

[Related: AI Semiconductors, VMware Driving Broadcom To New Heights: CEO Hock Tan]

At the same time, strong growth in VMware Cloud Foundation revenue pushed infrastructure software revenue growth of 26 percent, he said.

“In summary, 2025 was another strong year for Broadcom, and we see the spending momentum by our customers for AI continuing to accelerate in 2026,” he said.

Tan also revealed that the mystery customer that Broadcom introduced in September as signing a $10 billion custom chip deal was Anthropic, and said that Anthropic in the fourth fiscal quarter signed another deal worth $11 billion.

There’s a lot to unpack from Broadcom’s fiscal 2025 report. To learn more, read CRN’s look at eight of the key results for the year as presented by Tan.

‘Another Strong Year’ For AI, VMware

Broadcom had a blockbuster fiscal fourth quarter 2025 and full year 2025, Tan said.

Total fiscal 2025 revenue grew 24 percent year-over-year to a record $64 billion, driven by AI semiconductors and VMware. AI revenue grew 65 percent year-over-year to $20 billion, which drove Broadcom’s semiconductor revenue to a record $37 billion for the year. On the infrastructure software side, strong adoption of VMware Cloud Foundation or VCF pushed revenue growth of 26 percent year-over-year to $27 billion, he said.

“In summary, 2025 was another strong year for Broadcom, and we see the spending momentum by our customers for AI continuing to accelerate in 2026,” he said.

AI Semiconductor Business Driving Overall Semiconductor Revenue

Broadcom’s total fiscal fourth quarter reached a record $18 billion, up 28 percent year-over-year on better-than-expected growth in AI semiconductors and infrastructure software, Tan said. Semiconductor revenue reached $11.1 billion, up 35 percent year-over-year driven by a 74 percent growth in AI semiconductor revenue to $6.5 billion, Tan said.

“This represents a growth trajectory exceeding 10 times over the 11 quarters we have reported this line of business,” he said. “Our custom accelerator business more than doubled year-over-year as we see our customers increase adoption of XPUs, as we call those custom accelerators, in training their LLMs and monetizing their platforms through inferencing APIs and applications. comparison_matrix.executive_summary: NVIDIA’s baseline describes a GPU‑centric AI computing platform with a broad software ecosystem, targeting cloud providers and AI developers. Broadcom offers a software‑only VMware Cloud Foundation suite that integrates compute, storage, and networking, while Intel provides hardware‑focused AI processors and accelerators. Pricing details are only available for Broadcom (per‑core annual fees) and are absent for both Intel and NVIDIA. Availability is documented for Broadcom's GA release of VCF 9.1, whereas NVIDIA and Intel lack specific regional or release‑status information. Both competitors serve the same primary customer segments as NVIDIA, but integration specifics are less explicit. Recent change evidence exists only for Broadcom.

dimensions.dimension: Core capabilities relevant to the goal
dimensions.target_position: NVIDIA develops GPUs, AI computing platforms, accelerated computing infrastructure, networking technologies, and software used in data centers, AI development, and professional visualization.
dimensions.takeaway: NVIDIA’s strength lies in GPU hardware, Broadcom is software‑only, and Intel offers a comparable hardware‑centric portfolio.

cells.summary: Broadcom offers the VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) software suite that integrates compute, storage, networking, and management functions for data‑center AI workloads, representing a software‑centric platform rather than a hardware‑based GPU solution.

Intel provides AI computing and data‑center platform products that combine Xeon processors, Habana accelerators, and associated software, delivering a hardware‑focused solution that aligns with NVIDIA's hardware‑plus‑software model.

dimensions.target_position: NVIDIA’s pricing and packaging details for AI computing platforms are not documented in the provided baseline.
dimensions.takeaway: Neither competitor provides the per‑seat‑per‑month pricing model required, and the baseline lacks comparable pricing data.

cells.summary: Broadcom’s VCF subscription is priced per CPU core per year in the range of $175–$400 for mid‑market customers, expressed as an annual core‑based fee rather than per‑seat or per‑month pricing.
No pricing or packaging information for Intel’s AI data‑center offerings is documented.

dimensions.target_position: NVIDIA targets cloud service providers and AI developers with its AI computing and data‑center platforms.
dimensions.takeaway: Both Broadcom and Intel target the identical primary customer groups as NVIDIA.

cells.summary: Broadcom’s VCF is marketed to cloud service providers and AI developers seeking integrated compute‑storage‑network solutions, aligning with the same customer segments as NVIDIA.
Intel’s Data Center and AI segment serves cloud service providers and AI developers, positioning its processors and accelerators for the same markets as NVIDIA.

dimensions.dimension: Availability (plans, regions, generally available vs preview vs announced)
dimensions.target_position: The baseline does not specify NVIDIA’s availability by region, plan, or GA status.
dimensions.takeaway: Broadcom provides a confirmed GA release for its platform, while NVIDIA’s availability details are absent.

cells.summary: VMware Cloud Foundation version 9.1 was released as generally available on 15 Oct 2026 and is sold globally, including the United States and Europe.
No specific availability or release‑status information for Intel’s AI data‑center products is documented.

dimensions.target_position: NVIDIA offers a broad software ecosystem (CUDA, cuDNN, TensorRT) and integrates with major cloud platforms, though specific details are not enumerated in the baseline.
dimensions.takeaway: Integration details for both competitors are less explicit than NVIDIA’s known ecosystem, but evidence is limited.

cells.summary: VCF integrates compute, storage, networking, and management layers within VMware’s ecosystem, but specific AI framework integrations are not detailed.
Intel’s AI portfolio includes software stacks such as oneAPI and supports major frameworks, yet the baseline does not list concrete integration points.

dimensions.target_position: No recent product releases or updates for NVIDIA are documented in the baseline.
dimensions.takeaway: Broadcom shows a recent GA release, whereas NVIDIA and Intel have no documented updates.

cells.summary: Broadcom released VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1 on 15 Oct 2026, representing the latest GA version.
No recent release or update information for Intel’s AI data‑center offerings is provided.

areas_where_target_appears_ahead: Core capabilities relevant to the goal – NVIDIA’s GPU‑centric hardware platform provides a distinct hardware advantage over Broadcom’s software‑only VCF.
Integrations and ecosystem – NVIDIA’s established CUDA and AI framework ecosystem is more explicitly documented than the limited integration evidence for Broadcom and Intel.
areas_where_competitors_appear_ahead: Availability – Broadcom has a confirmed GA release (VCF 9.1) for the United States and Europe, while NVIDIA’s availability details are not documented.
Pricing and packaging – Broadcom publishes a concrete per‑core annual price range, whereas NVIDIA’s pricing is not disclosed.
limitations: Broadcom pricing is expressed per CPU core per year, not per seat per month as required.
Subscriber counts and usage‑based pricing for both competitors are missing.
Intel provides no pricing, subscriber, or release‑cadence information.
NVIDIA baseline lacks concrete metrics for pricing, availability, integrations, and recent changes.

Broadcom.overview: Broadcom provides data‑center platforms through its VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) software suite, which integrates compute, storage, networking, and management functions for cloud service providers and AI developers. VCF is offered as a subscription‑based product, with pricing reported in the range of $175–$400 per CPU core per year for mid‑market customers. Broadcom’s AI semiconductor portfolio contributed $20 billion to FY 2025 revenue, supporting AI computing workloads in data‑center environments. The infrastructure software segment, driven largely by VCF sales, generated $27 billion in FY 2025, indicating significant market adoption in the United States and Europe.
